memoryText: Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Romans 10:9 slowly, several times, and try to say it from memory. Then read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse is among the clearest statements in the New Testament of what it means to be saved.

“If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord.” The earliest Christian creed is three words: Jesus is Lord. In the Greek Old Testament, “Lord” (kyrios) was the word for the name of God. To say “Jesus is Lord” is to say that Jesus shares the identity of the LORD. It is also a statement of allegiance: he is my master. In a world where Caesar was called lord, it was a dangerous confession.

“And believe in your heart.” The faith that saves is not just agreement; it comes from the heart, the center of the person. It is trust, not just knowledge.

“That God raised him from the dead.” The resurrection is the center of the faith. It proves that Jesus is who he said he was, that his death was accepted, and that death has been defeated.

“You will be saved.” The promise is sure. Saved from the wrath, from sin’s power, and ultimately from death.

Notice that the verse joins heart and mouth. True faith naturally speaks. And verse 13 adds that it is open to all: everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.

When you doubt whether you are really saved, return to this verse and ask: do I confess that Jesus is Lord, and do I believe that God raised him from the dead? If so, you have the promise of God.
weekInReview: This week you saw the final stretch of Paul’s argument and the beginning of its application. In Romans 9, Paul grieved over Israel and taught that God’s word has not failed, because God’s purposes work by mercy and election, not by physical descent. Chapter 10 gave the message of faith: confess that Jesus is Lord, believe that God raised him from the dead, and call on his name, and faith comes from hearing the word of Christ. Chapter 11 asked whether God has rejected Israel and answered with the remnant, the olive tree, and the mystery of “all Israel,” ending in the doxology: from him and through him and to him are all things. Three psalms accompanied the reading: Psalm 19 on creation’s voice that goes out to all the earth, Psalm 116 on calling on the name of the LORD, and Psalm 117 on the nations praising. Romans 12 and 13 began the practical section, calling believers to offer themselves as a living sacrifice and to overcome evil with good.
reflectionQuestions: Paul had great sorrow and unceasing anguish for those who did not believe. Who in your life do you carry that kind of burden for? What is one concrete thing you will do to pray for or reach out to them?
Romans 10:9 says to confess Jesus is Lord and believe that God raised him from the dead. What does it mean in daily life for Jesus to be your Lord, and not only your Savior?
Romans 12:1 says to present your whole self as a living sacrifice because of God’s mercies. What part of your life is hardest to hand over? What mercy of God can you remember as you do so?
prayerPrompts: Confess Jesus as Lord, and thank him for raising him from the dead.
Thank him for the promise of salvation.
